articles.title: South Korea's KOSPI Plunges 8% as Samsung and SK Hynix Lead a Chip Rout - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: South Korea's KOSPI Plunges 8% as Samsung and SK Hynix Lead a Chip Rout  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
Seoul's circuit breakers tripped for the tenth time this year on October 15. By the end of the session, the two companies making the memory chips behind the AI boom had each lost a tenth of their value.
The Kospi tumbled 8% to 5,528.05 on Thursday, triggering South Korea's tenth market-wide circuit breaker of the year, according to a report from The Korea Herald. SK Hynix sank 11.35%, and Samsung Electronics dropped 9.70%. Samsung Electro-Mechanics, which supplies components for the same AI server boom, fell sharply as well.
You don't halt an entire national stock exchange over nothing. The selloff opened rough, down 5.59% at the bell, and kept sliding all morning. A sell-sidecar hit at 9:07 a.m., suspending index futures-linked program trades. By 12:38 p.m., the main circuit breaker kicked in and froze trading across the board for 20 minutes. When it reopened, the bleeding continued.
Here's the part that should worry anyone holding AI-adjacent stocks: this wasn't really about chip demand collapsing. It was about the cost of money. A hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation reading on October 14 pushed back bets on near-term Federal Reserve rate cuts, and that hit hardest at exactly the companies that have been borrowing the most to build AI infrastructure. CoreWeave's bond yields had already jumped toward 15% earlier in the week on the same fear. When financing costs rise, the math behind every chip megafab and every AI data center gets shakier, and investors in Seoul decided to sell first and ask questions later.
Samsung and SK Hynix didn't need a rate scare to feel exposed. Two days earlier, on October 12, shares in both companies had already slid after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies unveiled a new 4F² DRAM cell architecture at a conference in Shanghai. CXMT is targeting a server DDR5 module built on that design by the end of 2026. Samsung's own roadmap doesn't get there until 2028, according to industry estimates reported at the time.
South Korea's KOSPI crashed nearly 10% on June 23 after Broadcom's Q3 AI chip guidance of $16 billion missed Wall Street's $17.2 billion estimate, triggering a circuit breaker as Samsung and SK Hynix each fell more than 12%. The selloff exposed the KOSPI's dangerous concentration in two memory chip stocks and the fragility of a market priced for... - Broadcom guidance miss triggers Korean market - AI chip demand uncertainty spooks semiconductor
CXMT still holds less than 10% of global DRAM share against Samsung's roughly 39% and SK Hynix's 25%, and it has published no performance data or qualification results to back up the claim. The architecture itself is unproven at scale under the export controls that limit CXMT's access to advanced manufacturing tools. But the memory market doesn't need a Chinese rival to actually catch up this year. It just needs traders to believe the moat is two years thinner than they thought it was last month, and Samsung's and SK Hynix's stocks already carried the valuation of companies with no rival in sight.
Japan felt the contagion too. Kioxia, the memory maker spun out of Toshiba, sold off sharply the same day, a sign the selloff wasn't a Korea-only story but a read-through across the entire Asian memory supply chain that feeds Nvidia, Microsoft, and every other buyer racing to stock AI servers.
The same day, Taiwan told a different story
Here's the twist. While Seoul was tripping circuit breakers, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. held its own third-quarter earnings call, on the same Thursday, and the numbers it reported were not a crisis. TSMC posted record quarterly revenue of NT$1.494 trillion, up 50.9% from a year earlier, beating the top end of its own forecast. Nine-month revenue for 2026 hit NT$3.899 trillion, up 41.1% year over year. Management's message, in short: the AI chip boom isn't slowing down on the manufacturing side at all.
So which is it? Frankly, both readings can be true at once, and that's the uncomfortable part. TSMC makes the logic chips and sells to a broad base of customers who are still paying up for capacity. Samsung and SK Hynix sell memory, a market where a credible new entrant and a sudden spike in the cost of capital can both bite at the same time, even while the underlying demand for AI computing keeps climbing. The Kospi crash isn't proof that AI spending is cracking. It's proof that the stocks built on the assumption nothing could touch Korean memory dominance had very little room for bad news, and got two pieces of it in the same week.
Foreign investors had already been pulling back hard going into the crash, posting heavy net selling in South Korean equities in the prior session alone, alongside a jump in short-selling activity. That's capital voting with its feet before the circuit breaker ever tripped, and it's the clearest sign yet that the easy money in Korean chip stocks has started asking harder questions than it did a month ago.

articles.title: South Korea's earnings season kicks off next week; JPMorgan says memory chip pullback creates medium-term buying window - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: South Korea's earnings season kicks off next week; JPMorgan says memory chip pullback creates medium-term buying window  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
South Korea's third-quarter earnings season officially kicks off the week of October 19, and the recent deep correction in memory chip stocks is being viewed by Wall Street as a window for medium-term positioning. JPMorgan's Asia-Pacific equity research team concluded in its latest note that the memory sector has entered an "expectations reset quarter," and the current divergence between price and fundamentals offers investors an entry point to bet on an upcycle that is "longer and higher."
According to a research note published October 15 by JPMorgan analyst Jay Kwon and colleagues, last week's preliminary results from Samsung Electronics (in line), LG Electronics (below expectations), and LG Energy Solution (above expectations) set the tone for this earnings season. The report noted that after meeting with more than 100 investors across Asia, Kwon pointed out that memory stocks have fallen approximately 6% over the past month and 15% over the past three months, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) rose about 10% and fell about 4% over the same respective periods—a divergence that is creating a favorable risk-reward entry point for duration trades.
Hit by hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data overnight and mounting concerns over an AI valuation bubble, South Korean equities suffered a historic sell-off on October 15. Data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on October 14 showed September CPI rose 3.7% year-over-year, up from 3.4% previously, reigniting rate-hike fears; rising credit risk in AI infrastructure financing further amplified valuation concerns. South Korea's KOSPI closed at 5,554.22, down 7.57%, breaching the 5,600 level. Chip giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix led the decline, closing down more than 9% and 10%, respectively. The Korea Exchange activated a "sell-side sidecar" mechanism to halt programmatic sell orders and ease selling pressure.
The sell-off swept across major Asia-Pacific markets:
| Market | Close | Daily Change | 
|---|---|---|
| South Korea KOSPI | 5,554.22 | -7.57% | 
| South Korea KOSDAQ | 760.82 | -7.65% | 
| Nikkei 225 | 64,425.95 | -4.90% | 
| Taiwan Weighted Index | 46,969.87 | -3.41% | 
Note: Closing data as of October 15, 2026. The Taiwan Weighted Index fell 1,655.96 points, the sixth-largest single-day point decline in Taiwan market history.
Taiwan's market was not spared either: the weighted index lost the 47,000 level and its monthly moving average, with foreign investors selling a record NT$302.555 billion (approximately $9.3 billion) in a single day. TSMC fell NT$50 to close at NT$2,440, while ASE Technology and other packaging and testing interface names closed limit-down.
Expectations reset quarter: duration trade logic amid sentiment divergence
Jay Kwon met with more than 100 Asian investors in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur, and Hong Kong over the past two weeks. The findings reveal a key divergence: top-down conclusions about AI spending sustainability are clearly disconnected from bottom-up readings of memory supply-demand fundamentals, with investor sentiment sharply split.
JPMorgan had previously characterized Q3 as an "expectations reset quarter," noting that memory stocks could remain volatile in the near term due to a lack of immediate catalysts. On the data front, memory stocks are down roughly 6% over the past month and 15% over three months, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose about 10% and fell about 4% over the same periods—a stark contrast in trajectories.
However, the bank believes this very sentiment divergence and price dislocation provides a good entry point for "duration trades"—bets on a memory upcycle that is "longer and higher" from a medium-term perspective. Kwon added that from a medium-term view, the risk-reward has turned favorable, and he recommends investors accumulate on dips during the recent pullback.
Six overweight picks spanning the memory supply chain
Based on this assessment, JPMorgan identified its core overweight picks for the next six months, covering memory chips themselves as well as upstream and downstream ecosystem plays:
| Name | Segment | Ticker | 
|---|---|---|
| Samsung Electronics | Memory core | 005930.KS | 
| SK Hynix | Memory core | 000660.KS | 
| Kioxia | Memory | 285A.T | 
| Samsung Electro-Mechanics | MLCC & substrates | 009150.KS | 
| ISU | AI PCB | 007660.KS | 
| ISC | Test sockets | 095340.KQ | 
Note: List sourced from JPMorgan's October 15 research note; overweight horizon is six months.
This portfolio reflects a systematic approach to positioning across the entire memory supply chain's medium-term recovery, rather than a single-segment bet. From memory manufacturers to passive components, PCBs, and test-related equipment, it covers the full hardware chain driven by AI compute expansion.
Kioxia, the only Japanese company on the list, also plunged in Tokyo trading that day: it closed at ¥12,880 (approximately $82), down 12.32% on the day, and has fallen more than 30% from its post-split high of ¥19,750 (approximately $130) set on October 5. The Nikkei 225 fell 3,318 points that day, its third-largest single-day point decline in history. Kioxia is scheduled to report earnings on October 30, shortly after South Korea's earnings season begins, providing another checkpoint for the memory cycle thesis.
Validation framework and falsification conditions
JPMorgan also laid out a validation framework for its thesis. On the results front, the key question is whether earnings delivery from technology and life insurance sectors—slated as outperformers—beats sectors the bank has flagged as negative, as results roll in starting the week of October 19. On the mechanism front, marginal changes in memory spot prices, AI-related orders, and capital expenditure will be critical indicators of whether the "longer upcycle" duration thesis holds.
The bank also spelled out clear falsification conditions: if memory supply-demand continues to weaken, catalysts remain absent, or the earnings season brings widespread downward revisions, JPMorgan said it would withdraw the thesis. The validation window runs from October 19, 2026 through early November.
The logic can be summarized as follows:
For the South Korean market overall, this quarter's earnings season will not only determine near-term pricing in the memory sector but also serve as a key reference point for the health of the global semiconductor supply chain. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, as the two memory giants, will see their earnings performance and capex guidance directly test whether the AI-driven memory upcycle remains on track.

articles.title: South Korea's Stock Rout Reveals a Double Threat to the AI Boom - Business Insider
articles.summary: South Korea's Stock Rout Reveals a Double Threat to the AI Boom  Business Insider
articles.full_text:
South Korea's stock market is bearing the brunt of a global AI selloff as investors question whether massive spending on the technology will pay off and worry that persistently high interest rates will make the boom more expensive to sustain.
On Thursday, the benchmark Kospi index ended 8% lower, while Samsung Electronics and memory-chip rival SK Hynix closed 9% and 11% lower, respectively.
The plunge followed a tech-led selloff on Wall Street on Wednesday after hotter-than-expected US inflation data revived concerns about higher interest rates.
The selloff spread across Asia's other major AI markets. Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 5% lower, with chipmaker Kioxia and tech investor SoftBank Group among the biggest losers. Taiwan's Taiex fell 3%, as chipmaking giant TSMC lost 2%.
The regional rout comes as investors increasingly question the valuations of AI-linked stocks
Investors are increasingly questioning how much they should pay for semiconductor stocks, even as the companies' earnings outlook remains relatively strong.
Doubts about the profitability of leading AI companies and their growing reliance on external financing were prompting investors to rethink how they valued chipmakers, wrote Mingyu Kim, an analyst at KB Securities, wrote on Wednesday.
"Concerns over the sustainability of AI investment beyond the next 12 months have prompted the market to revert to valuing semiconductor stocks as commodity-driven cyclicals," Kim wrote.
Even blockbuster earnings have failed to reassure investors. '
Last Thursday, Samsung Electronics forecast a nearly ninefold increase in third-quarter operating profit, but its shares have since lost nearly a fifth of their value.
Competition is another concern. Chinese chipmaker CXMT plans to unveil a new server-memory product by year-end, raising fears that greater supply could pressure chip prices.
Meanwhile, foreign investors sold more than 12 trillion won of South Korean stocks on a net basis in October, according to KB Securities. Buybacks by Samsung and SK Hynix, which had helped support the market since August, are also winding down, leaving fewer buyers to cushion the decline.
The latest selloff adds to a year of extraordinary swings in South Korean stocks.
The Kospi more than doubled in the first half before plunging 22% in July, its worst month since the 2008 global financial crisis.
The index had fallen about 35% since the end of June, going from the world's best-performing major market in the first half to its worst performer in the second.
Still, KB Securities sees a potential buying opportunity as the market searches for a bottom.
"We believe the market is currently searching for the second bottom of a W-shaped recovery," Kim wrote.

articles.title: EU Moves to Lift China Sanctions to Save German Chipmaking Materials Supplier - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: EU Moves to Lift China Sanctions to Save German Chipmaking Materials Supplier  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
BEIJING — The European Union is seeking to lift sanctions on a Chinese company in order to rescue a German semiconductor parts maker pushed to the brink of collapse by China's rare earth restrictions.
At high-level trade talks held in Beijing on the 8th and 9th of this month, the EU and China discussed lifting trade restrictions imposed on a Chinese company accused of supporting Russia's war, in exchange for China lifting sanctions it had imposed on Germany's Sindlhauser Materials, Bloomberg reported on the 14th. Sindlhauser is a small and medium-sized company specializing in precision semiconductor manufacturing and advanced coatings.
The EU had earlier sanctioned the Chinese company on grounds that it supplied key components used in weapons production to Russia. China retaliated in July by placing 14 European companies, including Sindlhauser, on its export control list. Sindlhauser relies entirely on supplies of Chinese rare earths and critical minerals and is reportedly at risk of shutting down within months if the Chinese sanctions remain in place.
The targeting of a little-known German small business shows how meticulously China is moving to weaponize its resources, analysts say. Over the past year and a half, China has used licensing requirements for critical minerals and rare earth exports to gather extensive information on global supply chains. Foreign companies are required to submit detailed materials, including information on their end customers, how Chinese raw materials are used and photographs of final products. That has allowed China to identify and precisely strike vulnerable links in the supply chain of Europe's semiconductor industry, according to one analysis.
Bloomberg noted that German companies are handing over trade secrets to China while the German government cannot obtain even a comparable level of information, adding that the more serious problem is that Berlin has not even developed a strategy to address this gap in economic intelligence-gathering capability.

China and North Korea have officially opened their most significant land border crossing, more than a decade after the bridge was completed.
The 3-kilometre New Yalu River Bridge, which links the Chinese city of Dandong with North Korea, was finished in 2014 but had remained unused until Thursday.
Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported that the two countries held an opening ceremony.
Trucks carrying Chinese flags lined up on the bridge ahead of the first crossings, while crowds gathered on the Chinese side to watch.
The opening is a sign of improving ties between Beijing and Pyongyang, whose leaders have held two summits in the past year.
China is by far North Korea’s largest trading partner, despite UN sanctions over Pyongyang’s missile and nuclear weapons programmes.
China’s exports to North Korea rose 25 per cent last year to $2.3 billion, a six-year high but still well below levels before sanctions were tightened in 2017.
Analysts say the bridge is unlikely to bring an immediate return to pre-sanctions trade levels, but will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products needed for North Korea’s development projects.

articles.title: Musk Says China Will Mass-Produce Memory Chips by 2028, Praises Micron's Pricing While Taking Aim at Korean Rivals - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Musk Says China Will Mass-Produce Memory Chips by 2028, Praises Micron's Pricing While Taking Aim at Korean Rivals  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on social platform X on October 15 that China will produce large volumes of memory (RAM) by 2028, remarks that came as South Korean memory-related stocks tumbled and markets worried about Chinese semiconductor makers accelerating their catch-up. In his post, he directly responded to a Korean financial column's warning about memory oversupply risks and suggested that South Korea's semiconductor industry has only a two-to-three-year window to transform.
Musk's post was a commentary on an analysis by a Korean financial columnist. The column warned that as new Chinese capacity comes online, South Korea could face a memory oversupply situation by 2029, and that if the local industry fails to cultivate new growth engines within the next two to three years, its existing cyclical advantages could reverse.
Micron's Pricing Strategy Wins Praise, Korean Chipmakers Implicitly Criticized
Just one day before this post (October 14), Musk had already publicly endorsed Micron Technology's (MU) pricing strategy on X. He said Micron's attitude toward future memory prices is quite reasonable and that the company is making smart moves to win customers' long-term loyalty; by contrast, other suppliers are charging unacceptably high prices. He stated bluntly: "This is something customers never forget."
While Musk did not explicitly name the "other suppliers," the global DRAM market has long been dominated by three players—Samsung Electronics (005930.KS), SK Hynix (000660.KS), and Micron—and Korean media widely interpreted the remarks as targeting the two South Korean semiconductor giants.
Industry sources noted that the trigger for Musk's comments was a recently published JPMorgan research report with a bullish outlook on the memory industry. The report argued that the global memory supply-demand imbalance could persist through 2028, and Musk, in responding to related discussions, took the opportunity to express dissatisfaction with supplier pricing behavior.
JPMorgan: Memory Shortage to Persist Through 2028
JPMorgan said in its report that memory market fundamentals are "significantly stronger than 90 days ago," with demand currently far exceeding supply. The firm estimates memory supply shortfalls of approximately 20% in 2026, 19% in 2027, and 15% in 2028.
The growth outlook for the High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) market is similarly bullish. JPMorgan projects the HBM market will expand from approximately $64 billion (about NT$2.1 trillion) in 2026 to approximately $160 billion (about NT$5.2 trillion) in 2027, and further climb to $280 billion (about NT$9.1 trillion) by 2028.
| Year | Memory Supply Shortfall | HBM Market Size Estimate | 
|---|---|---|
| 2026 | 20% | $64 billion | 
| 2027 | 19% | $160 billion | 
| 2028 | 15% | $280 billion | 
Note: Figures cited from JPMorgan research report, covering global memory market supply-demand gap and HBM market size projections.
On the supply contract front, Micron's long-term customer agreements have increased from 16 to 26, extending through 2030 and covering more than 35% of company revenue, with remaining performance obligations totaling $150 billion (about NT$4.9 trillion). Additionally, more than 75% of Micron's fiscal 2027 output has already been committed by customers.
Under supply-constrained conditions, memory makers are locking substantial capacity into long-term contracts. The coverage disclosed by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix is as follows:
| Supplier | Long-Term Contract Coverage | Disclosed Details | 
|---|---|---|
| Micron | Over 75% of FY2027 output | 26 long-term agreements, $150 billion in remaining performance obligations | 
| Samsung Electronics | Nearly 80% of 2027 output (including HBM) | Signed with 5 major data center customers | 
| SK Hynix | Over 10 customers, contracts of approximately 5 years | Disclosed at July earnings call | 
Note: Micron figures disclosed in September 30, 2026 earnings; Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix figures disclosed at their respective earnings calls.
Market strategy analyst Shay Boloor pointed out on X that when supply eventually loosens, Micron has an opportunity to convert this "goodwill" that Musk described into longer-term contracts and higher market share.
China's Technology Catch-Up Rattles Markets
Musk had also noted days earlier that once China masters the manufacturing technology for a product, its ability to scale production often exceeds the rest of the world combined, citing lithium batteries and solar panels as examples.
He further analyzed that memory was a low-margin, standardized commodity about three years ago, and that LPDDR5 and LPDDR6 use common specifications, with China appearing to be rapidly mastering the relevant technologies. However, he believes that next-generation HBM architectures, SRAM layers, and thermal challenges in 3D-stacked RAM remain technical hurdles that are harder for Chinese manufacturers to overcome.
Market concerns about the rise of China's memory industry are not unfounded. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced at the 4th Integrated Circuit and Chiplet Conference held October 9–10 that it has achieved key progress in developing its next-generation 4F² DRAM architecture, with plans to launch DDR5 RDIMM server memory combining 4F² architecture with hybrid bonding technology by year-end, directly targeting the server market. This news has already had a significant impact on the stock prices of major global memory companies.
Current mainstream DRAM uses 6F² architecture, where each memory cell occupies an area equivalent to six times the square of the minimum feature size; 4F² reduces cell area by roughly one-third, theoretically enabling approximately 50% higher storage density at the same wafer area and process node. ChangXin's core technology is its independently developed vertical surrounding gate (VSG) transistor, which uses a vertical structure to improve gate control and reduce leakage and short-channel effects; hybrid bonding separates DRAM and CMOS processes before re-integrating them in three dimensions. ChangXin has invested years in 4F² research, with over 300 published patent families, while SK Hynix only announced a similar technology roadmap in 2025, and Samsung plans to mass-produce sub-10nm DRAM using this architecture only in 2028—if ChangXin delivers on schedule by year-end, it would lead Korean rivals by about two years in memory cell architecture product timing.
However, ChangXin's entry this time targets system main memory, which remains a different technology tier from the High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) used alongside AI accelerators; server DDR5 RDIMMs must also complete compatibility validation and burn-in testing with processor makers, and subsequent mass-production capability remains to be verified.
On Monday (October 12), Micron's market value shrank by approximately $52 billion (about NT$1.7 trillion), SK Hynix's market value fell by approximately $41.5 billion (about NT$1.3 trillion), and SanDisk's market value contracted by approximately $15 billion (about NT$490 billion). This sell-off was driven by multiple overlapping factors. On the same day, South Korean stocks played catch-up after the Hangul Day holiday, with the KOSPI plunging 3.65% and Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix shares both falling about 4.5%; additionally, Samsung and SK Hynix's combined buyback program of approximately ₩55 trillion (about $40 billion)—the largest in Korean history—ended early, removing a key source of buying support for semiconductor stocks.
| Company | Single-Day Market Value Loss | 
|---|---|
| Micron Technology | Approximately $52 billion | 
| SK Hynix | Approximately $41.5 billion | 
| SanDisk | Approximately $15 billion | 
Note: Figures represent single-trading-day market value changes on October 12, 2026, as markets simultaneously digested China's memory technology progress, Korean market catch-up selling, and the end of the buyback program.
On the stock price front, Micron fell 3.62% on Tuesday (October 13) to close at $953.19 (about NT$31,000), then rose 0.32% in after-hours trading to $956.20. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 0.23% that day, marking its fifth consecutive session of declines.
Implications for Taiwan's Supply Chain
This wave of memory price increases is not entirely bad news for Taiwanese companies. Taiwan's DRAM maker Nanya Technology (2408) reported third-quarter self-assessed financials on October 12, with revenue reaching NT$133.649 billion (approximately $4.1 billion), up 62% quarter-over-quarter and 612% year-over-year, with gross margin of 85.7%, up another 6.2 percentage points from the previous quarter. Management also expects 2027 contract prices to maintain double-digit increases, with gross margin staying above 80%. Nanya's product lineup centers on DDR5, DDR4, and low-power memory—precisely the commodity DRAM battlefield that ChangXin is targeting—making it the most directly exposed to this China capacity issue. Winbond Electronics (2344), which focuses on niche DRAM and NOR flash memory, has a different product mix and application market, so the competitive dynamics in server DDR5 cannot be directly applied to its entire business. As for module makers on the procurement side such as ADATA (3260) and Team Group (4967), the impact depends on certification, procurement costs, and inventory changes from new supply sources.
A more direct change for Taiwanese readers is that Taiwanese PC brands Acer and Asus, as well as HP, have already adopted ChangXin memory chips in some PC products—Chinese DRAM is moving from a fringe role into the bill of materials for mainstream consumer products.
Industry Landscape Faces Restructuring Pressure
The timing of Musk's remarks is particularly sensitive. South Korea's memory industry is facing structural competitive pressure from China, and Musk—as the head of the world's largest electric vehicle maker and a major customer of AI infrastructure—has added a new variable

articles.title: China and North Korea open New Yalu River Bridge, state media reports - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: China and North Korea open New Yalu River Bridge, state media reports  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
China and North Korea have officially opened the New Yalu River Bridge, also called the Amnok River bridge, China’s state-run Xinhua news agency reports.
In a video address at the opening ceremony on Thursday, China’s Premier Li Qiang said relations between the two countries “are entering a new stage and opening a new chapter”, Xinhua reported.
Li said the cross-border infrastructure project was championed by Chinese President Xi Jinping and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Li said the bridge’s opening will strongly promote bilateral economic and trade cooperation while also further strengthening people-to-people exchanges and the emotional bonds between the two countries.
At the opening ceremony, Pak Thae Song, the premier of the North Korean cabinet said the bridge would accelerate the prosperity of the two countries and the well-being of both populations, adding new momentum to a mutually beneficial economic cooperation, North Korea’s state media KCNA said on Friday.
According to KCNA, Pak Thae Song emphasized North Korea’s consistent stance towards advancing North Korea-China relations.
China completed its side of the bridge in 2014, hoping to boost trade ties. However, North Korea left its side unfinished for years as relations soured after Beijing supported United Nations sanctions over Pyongyang’s nuclear tests.
The first bridge connecting Russia and North Korea opened earlier this month.
China-North Korea relations
China’s exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3bn last year, 25 percent up from the previous year. Xi was welcomed in Pyongyang in June for the first time since 2019.
Since 2018, Beijing has tried to repair ties with Pyongyang, which also briefly began improving relations with Washington around the same time.
The China-North Korea relationship was forged during the Korean War. In 1961, the two countries signed the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which remains China’s only formal military alliance.
The treaty contains a mutual defence clause committing either side to assist the other if one comes under armed attack.
Although China was North Korea’s main diplomatic partner and protector for decades, relations strained after Beijing in 2017 supported tightening sanctions on Pyongyang for its nuclear weapons programme.
Analysts say North Korea’s recent growing relationship with Russia may have changed the balance of Pyongyang’s diplomatic dependence, reducing its reliance on Beijing.
North Korea and Russia signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in 2024, including a mutual defence provision. Military and political ties between the two countries have grown considerably stronger, with North Korea deploying thousands of troops to fight in Russia’s war on Ukraine.
United States President Donald Trump also signalled interest in repairing relations with Pyongyang last month, after his talks with Kim abruptly ended in 2019. In his second term, Trump has floated meeting Kim again, though no official meeting has been set.
North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, exchanges with China could involve goods North Korea needs to develop its civilian economy, according to analysts.

articles.title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay - BBC
articles.summary: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay  BBC
articles.full_text:
A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme.
The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them.
Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang, in a video address on Thursday, said the bridge was a "new landmark symbolising the traditional friendship between China and North Korea", and that the two countries were "opening a new chapter" in bilateral ties.
The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region.
The new bridge is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges".
Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea.
A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC.
"Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds.
"China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually."
Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong.
But the alliance is not without tension.
Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan.
China's attitude has shifted more recently.
"Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC.
Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war.
At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops.
Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day.
So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties.
Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
"But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing."

articles.title: Kospi hits the brakes: South Korean benchmark plunges 7.5%, triggers 'sidecar' stop for investors - The Times of India
articles.summary: Kospi hits the brakes: South Korean benchmark plunges 7.5%, triggers 'sidecar' stop for investors  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s stock market hit a rough patch on Thursday, with the benchmark Kospi plunging 7.49% as technology stocks came under heavy selling pressure. The rout spread across Asian markets, prompting the country’s exchange operator to trigger a five-minute trading halt on programme sell orders after a sharp drop in index futures.
The KOSPI dropped 450.02 points to 5,558.79, putting it on course for a seventh consecutive session of losses, its longest losing streak since September 2024. The index has fallen nearly 35% from its record high in June.
The pressure on Asian equities followed a technology-led sell-off on Wall Street after US consumer price inflation accelerated more than expected in September. The data fuelled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates later this year, putting technology companies and AI-related stocks under further pressure.
MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan fell 3.3%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 declined 4.8%. S&P 500 e-mini futures were down 0.5%.
Samsung, SK Hynix lead South Korean market rout
Major technology companies accounted for some of the steepest losses on the South Korean exchange. Samsung Electronics shares fell 9.05%, while SK Hynix dropped 11.06%, reflecting the broader weakness across Asia’s semiconductor supply chain.
Battery maker LG Energy Solution lost 3.44%. Hyundai Motor declined 3.99%, while sister automaker Kia Corp fell 2.03%.
The selling extended to other Asian technology companies. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fell 2%, while Japan’s memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings plunged more than 11%. SoftBank Group, an investor in AI, declined 9.4%.
Market breadth in South Korea remained heavily negative. Of the 889 stocks traded, 768 declined and 90 advanced. Foreign investors sold shares worth a net 355.6 billion won.
The won, meanwhile, strengthened 0.21% to 1,339.5 per dollar on the onshore settlement platform, compared with its previous close of 1,342.3.
‘Sidecar’ triggered
The sharp decline prompted the South Korean exchange operator to activate a sell-side “sidecar”, an automatic mechanism designed to temporarily cool trading during periods of heavy selling. The measure suspends program sell orders for five minutes after steep losses in index futures.
The trigger came as the KOSPI extended its decline to seven consecutive sessions. The benchmark has now shed nearly 35% since its June record, with retail investors among those hit hardest during a sell-off in July, when the index fell around 20%. Losses in highly leveraged single-stock exchange-traded funds (ETFs) contributed to the damage during that period.
The sell-off in Asia followed Wall Street’s third consecutive session of losses. The S&P 500 declined 1.1% overnight, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.9%. A gauge of semiconductor stocks recorded its sixth straight day of losses as investors reassessed the outlook for companies sensitive to borrowing costs.
Meanwhile, in South Korea’s bond market, December futures on three-year treasury bonds rose 0.12 point to 103.00. The yield on the most liquid three-year Korean treasury bond fell 3 basis points to 3.855%, while the benchmark 10-year yield declined 2.1 basis points to 4.224%.
Oil prices also moved lower, with Brent crude falling 1.7% to $104.20 a barrel. Traders weighed the potential impact of US sanctions relief on oil supply against attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Trucks line up as long-delayed China-North Korea bridge officially opens - The Standard (HK)
articles.summary: Trucks line up as long-delayed China-North Korea bridge officially opens  The Standard (HK)
articles.full_text:
China and North Korea officially marked the long-delayed opening of their most significant land border crossing on Thursday, aiming to rejuvenate trade and commerce after years of soured ties and pandemic-related disruptions to cross-border exchange.
The 3-km (2-mile) New Yalu River Bridge and the Chinese customs at the end of the 1.3-km crossing saw increased activity over the past few days, with trucks adorned with Chinese flags waiting on the bridge ahead of a crossing on Thursday.
Crowds also gathered on the Chinese side along a road overlooking the bridge.
Chinese and North Korean flags also lined the cable-stayed bridge with towering pylons that had been completed in 2014 but remained unused, while approach roads and a customs compound on the North Korea end remained unfinished.
On Thursday, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported the countries held an opening ceremony for the new bridge. North Korea's state media have yet to report on the scheduled event.
The opening signals progress in bilateral relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, marked by two summit meetings between their leaders in the past year.
China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers to and from North Korea over the country's defiant missile and nuclear weapons development.
China and Russia, two UN Security Council permanent member states that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
Analysts said North Korea, despite the potential economic boost from active trade, remains cautious of greater dependence on China. Russia is accused by countries such as the US and South Korea of supplying sensitive military assistance to the North in return for Pyongyang's help in fighting the war in Ukraine.
"The bridge is unlikely to lead immediately to a full-scale return to pre-sanctions trade," said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
But the bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products needed for North Korea's development projects, he said.
China's exports to North Korea rose to a six-year high of $2.3 billion last year, a 25% increase over the previous year. That was still well below levels before UN sanctions were tightened in 2017.

articles.title: China Closes In on Korean Chipmakers in NAND and DRAM - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: China Closes In on Korean Chipmakers in NAND and DRAM  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
China's push into semiconductors has advanced to the point where it is breathing down Korea's neck. Yangtze Memory Technologies, China's largest NAND flash maker, climbed to third place in global NAND shipments in the second quarter, overtaking Japan's Kioxia and the U.S.-based Micron Technology, according to research firm Counterpoint on the 16th. Its share of NAND revenue reached 14%, closing in on Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) at 28% and SK hynix (000660.KS) at 19%. Having focused until now on commodity NAND, Yangtze Memory is expanding into higher-margin enterprise products, signaling a head-to-head contest with Korean firms.
The picture is much the same in DRAM. ChangXin Memory Technologies, China's leading DRAM maker, recently declared with confidence that it will release products this year using 4F², a next-generation cell structure. Samsung Electronics is developing the same technology with mass production targeted for around 2028, meaning ChangXin would be two years ahead. That amounts to a declaration of war on the next-generation DRAM market. Some view it as overblown technology marketing, but advanced capabilities built up in such a short span can only sound an alarm for Korea's chip industry.
What makes China's rapid progress most threatening is that it has come under U.S. export controls and a technology blockade. Washington has identified Chinese semiconductors as a core threat to its economy, security and military, and has layered on restrictions: limits on advanced artificial intelligence chip exports, controls on chipmaking equipment, sanctions on individual companies and coordination with allies. China, for its part, is pressing ahead through astronomical policy funding, the training of science and engineering talent, deregulation and the localization of technology. Apple CEO John Ternus, speaking the same day about the memory supply crunch, said the company would "keep all options in mind" — a remark widely read as hinting at the possible use of Chinese-made memory, and one that underscores China's changed standing in chips.
What is required of us now is the courage to face reality and a firm will to respond. The government, the political establishment and companies alike must tighten their guard and stake everything on developing technology that keeps Korea far ahead. Remaining trapped in outdated ideological frames — viewing support for large companies with suspicion, or putting off regulatory reform such as greater labor flexibility — is a road to self-destruction. We must not forget that a moment's complacency or even a small policy error leads straight to being left behind.

Executive Summary — Principal Assessment
North Korea’s efforts to develop a submarine-based nuclear strike capability represent an increasingly consequential challenge to regional deterrence, not because Pyongyang has demonstrated a fully operational nuclear submarine force, but because it is seeking to diversify its nuclear delivery systems while developing a substantially closer military relationship with Russia.
The reported underwater launch of two different types of cruise missiles on 14 October 2026 indicates further progress in the integration of submarine weapons systems. South Korean military assessments support the occurrence of the launches and indicate the use of different launch arrangements. However, neither the operational readiness of the submarine concerned nor the nuclear status of its missile payloads has been independently established.
The more important strategic issue lies beyond the individual missile tests. North Korea’s defence-industrial relationship with Russia has evolved from conventional military cooperation into a broader exchange involving military equipment, operational experience, technical knowledge and material resources. Evidence collected by the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) identifies Russian transfers of air-defence systems, electronic-warfare equipment and ballistic-missile performance feedback to North Korea. These findings demonstrate that military technology exchange is already taking place, although they do not establish a transfer of submarine nuclear propulsion technology.
Russia is the most consequential potential external source of advanced submarine-related assistance. Moscow possesses the technological capabilities relevant to Pyongyang’s ambitions, has demonstrated a willingness to supply restricted military equipment, and has a strong incentive to reward North Korean support for its war against Ukraine. Nevertheless, the distinction between a plausible supplier and a verified transfer remains essential.
China occupies a different position. Beijing remains central to North Korea’s economic resilience but has competing interests in avoiding nuclear instability, uncontrolled proliferation and greater American military involvement in Northeast Asia. Chinese involvement in submarine technology transfers cannot be assumed from its political and economic relationship with Pyongyang.
The strategic danger for Washington, Seoul and Tokyo is therefore cumulative: even a limited North Korean submarine-launched missile capability could increase surveillance burdens and crisis uncertainty; a future improvement in propulsion, acoustic performance, missile integration and command systems would create a substantially more difficult deterrence problem.
The decisive intelligence question is whether North Korea can transform isolated technological demonstrations into a reliably deployable and survivable undersea weapons force—and whether external support can shorten that transition.

North Korea’s pursuit of a submarine-based nuclear capability exposes a strategic contradiction that Washington, Seoul and European governments can no longer assess separately: Russia’s dependence on North Korean military supplies is creating opportunities for technological cooperation that could strengthen Pyongyang’s future nuclear deterrent, while forcing Western allies to allocate additional resources across two increasingly connected security theatres. The underwater cruise-missile tests reported on 15 October 2026 make that contradiction immediate. They demonstrate further weapons-system development, not an operationally proven nuclear submarine force. The distinction matters because Russia has already supplied North Korea with military equipment and missile-related technical assistance, while the transfer of submarine nuclear propulsion technology remains unconfirmed. For allied governments, the financial and security consequences depend on whether this established military partnership begins eliminating the industrial constraints that have historically limited North Korea’s strategic naval ambitions.

The military relationship between Moscow and Pyongyang has moved beyond the conventional exchange of diplomatic support. The Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, signed on 19 June 2024, established a formal framework for bilateral assistance, including provisions concerning military support in circumstances defined by Article 4. The treaty gave institutional continuity to a relationship that Russia’s war against Ukraine had already made operationally valuable.
The scale of North Korean assistance explains why Pyongyang has acquired greater bargaining relevance. The Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT) reported in May 2025 that participating-state assessments identified transfers to Russia of as many as 9 million artillery and rocket rounds during 2024, at least 100 ballistic missiles, and the deployment of more than 11,000 North Korean military personnel by late 2024. These quantities represent physical contributions to Russian military operations, not a financial valuation of the bilateral relationship. Their significance lies in the negotiating position created by sustained wartime supply.
Russia possesses technological resources that North Korea cannot readily reproduce, particularly in advanced naval propulsion, military electronics and complex weapons integration. The May 2025 MSMT report identified Russian transfers of air-defence and electronic-warfare equipment, together with technical feedback concerning North Korean ballistic-missile performance. According to participating-state information, Russian feedback contributed to improvements in missile guidance. That finding establishes an important precedent: Moscow has already provided militarily relevant technical assistance, although the report does not establish the transfer of submarine nuclear propulsion equipment.
This creates an asymmetrical exchange. Pyongyang can provide ammunition and personnel with relatively immediate battlefield value, while Moscow can potentially supply selected technologies whose benefits accumulate over longer development cycles. Moscow might benefit from that pressure without transferring an entire submarine. It would nevertheless face the risks associated with disseminating sensitive technology and strengthening a nuclear-armed partner whose future decisions it cannot fully control.

articles.title: Rapidus Is the Last Chance for Japan to Matter in Semiconductors - JAPAN Forward
articles.summary: Rapidus Is the Last Chance for Japan to Matter in Semiconductors  JAPAN Forward
articles.full_text:
Japan has committed roughly $15 billion in government support to Rapidus, a semiconductor manufacturer established in 2022, in an ambitious effort to revive the country's advanced chipmaking industry. The company aims to begin mass production of cutting-edge 2-nanometer chips in the second half of fiscal 2027.
Rapidus has already made progress toward that goal, including opening a pilot production line at its Hokkaido factory and demonstrating its ability to produce prototype 2-nanometer transistors.
However, manufacturing chips on a commercial scale is a much greater challenge. The company must prove it can consistently produce large quantities of working chips at a competitive cost and convince customers to order.
Kazuto Suzuki, a professor of science and technology policy at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Public Policy and director of the Institute of Geoeconomics, believes Japan's investment is justified.
However, speaking to Japan Forward, he emphasized that Rapidus should not be viewed primarily as a safeguard against a potential conflict over Taiwan.
Two Halves of One Strategy
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker, has also been expanding its presence in Japan. Its first factory in Kumamoto Prefecture began mass production in late 2024, while a second is under development.
Suzuki sees TSMC's investment and Rapidus as serving two different purposes in Japan's economic security strategy.
Rapidus aims to make Japan an indispensable part of the global semiconductor supply chain by producing advanced chips. TSMC's factories, meanwhile, are intended to strengthen Japan's ability to meet domestic demand without relying entirely on imports.
Japan once dominated the semiconductor industry, accounting for roughly 50% of the global market in the 1980s. Today, its share is below 10%, and Suzuki believes time is running out to reverse the decline.
"I think this is going to be the last opportunity for Japan to take a gamble to be a meaningful player in the global market," he said.
The biggest concern is the loss of expertise. Engineers who helped build Japan's semiconductor industry are approaching retirement, taking decades of practical knowledge with them. Suzuki argues that younger engineers trained overseas cannot easily replace that experience.
"In the semiconductor world, experience is everything," he said.
That experience is particularly important for improving production yields, the percentage of chips manufactured on a silicon wafer that function properly.
Because wafers are expensive to produce, even small yield improvements can make a major difference to profitability. Suzuki praised the government's decision to bring in Atsuyoshi Koike, now Rapidus CEO, to lead the effort to rebuild Japan's chipmaking capabilities.
Two-Pronged Semiconductor Strategy
Suzuki said Rapidus could eventually rival TSMC's technological capabilities but operates under a different business model and isn't intended to replace it.
Japan's major chip buyers, including Sony, Denso, and Toyota, have limited demand for the cutting-edge processors Rapidus plans to manufacture.
Unlike companies producing AI servers and smartphone processors, they generally rely on less advanced chips. Rapidus will therefore depend largely on overseas customers.
The first plant began mass production in late 2024, producing 12- to 28-nanometer chips used in automobiles and industrial equipment.
TSMC is also expanding its advanced chipmaking capabilities in Japan. Its second Kumamoto plant is now planned to produce 3-nanometer chips, with operations expected to begin in 2028.
The Japanese government has approved subsidies of up to ¥732 billion ($4.7 billion) for the project, which Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has described as significant for economic security.
Who Will Fill the Fab?
Suzuki is optimistic about Rapidus finding customers. With demand for advanced chips surging because of AI and supplies struggling to keep pace, he believes "One way or another, there'll be customers from all over the world."
He also sees mass production as a necessary step, not a major obstacle. Private investors, he explained, are largely waiting for Rapidus to demonstrate its manufacturing capabilities before committing more funds.
In February, Rapidus raised ¥267.6 billion ($1.7 billion), including ¥167.6 billion from 32 private companies, exceeding its ¥130 billion target. CEO Koike has said the company is in talks with more than 60 potential customers.
However, questions remain about whether Rapidus can secure enough customers to make its business profitable. On October 5, the company announced partnerships with 17 firms, including Synopsys and Infosys, to help customers design chips. While this marks progress, it does not necessarily translate into orders.
Convincing customers to switch from established manufacturers such as TSMC will also be difficult, particularly given Rapidus's lack of a commercial production track record. Still, the company could attract smaller customers whose orders larger manufacturers prioritize less.
Success Is Measured in Yield
Suzuki offers a simple test for the whole policy. "If you make a good chip, then that's a success," he said. "If you improve the yield, that's a success."
Rapidus reached an important milestone in July 2025 when its prototype 2-nanometer transistors demonstrated the expected electrical performance. However, the company has not yet disclosed its production yield, a key measure of how many chips it can manufacture successfully.
Consistently producing advanced chips at a commercially viable cost remains a major challenge. Rapidus aims to begin mass production in fiscal 2027 and is targeting a stock market listing around fiscal 2031.
Suzuki believes it is too early to judge the company's prospects, with mass production providing the first meaningful test.
"It's still wait and see," he said. "But so far, Rapidus has been on schedule, and this is important."

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) reported record third-quarter earnings on October 15, even as South Korea's stock market suffered one of its sharpest declines of the year. The contrasting developments highlight a growing divide between the strong operating performance of leading semiconductor manufacturers and investors' concerns about the sustainability of global artificial intelligence investment.
TSMC reported net income of NT$763.06 billion (approximately US$23.6 billion), up 68.7% from a year earlier. Quarterly revenue increased 50.9% to NT$1.49 trillion, equivalent to US$46.72 billion. The results reflected continued demand for advanced semiconductors used in AI computing and other high-performance applications.
In Seoul, the benchmark KOSPI plunged 7.57% to close at 5,554.22 on the same day. Samsung Electronics fell 9.5%, while SK hynix declined 11.1%, as investors sold semiconductor stocks amid concerns over persistent US inflation, higher interest rates and the financial sustainability of AI infrastructure expansion.
Strong chip demand, rising investment concerns
TSMC's earnings suggest that demand for advanced semiconductor manufacturing remains strong. Technologies at 7 nanometers and below accounted for 79% of the company's third-quarter wafer revenue, underscoring the importance of advanced manufacturing processes in its business.
The Korean market's sharp decline, however, reflected a different set of concerns. Investors are increasingly examining whether the companies financing AI data centers and computing infrastructure can generate sufficient revenue and cash flow to justify their spending.
This distinction matters because semiconductor suppliers and AI infrastructure operators occupy different positions in the investment cycle. Chipmakers can recognize revenue as customers purchase processors and related components, while data center operators and AI service providers may need years to recover their infrastructure investments.
Strong demand for chips therefore does not automatically guarantee attractive returns for every company involved in the AI industry.
Why Korean semiconductor stocks came under pressure
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix are major participants in the global semiconductor supply chain, but their share prices remain sensitive to broader investor sentiment, foreign capital flows and expectations for future AI spending.
The October 15 selloff followed weakness in US technology shares, where concerns about inflation and the cost of financing had already weighed on AI-related stocks. Foreign investors were net sellers of approximately 3.6 trillion won in the Korean market, adding pressure to domestic equities.
The KOSPI's intraday decline also triggered a circuit breaker, temporarily halting trading for 20 minutes. The scale of the fall demonstrated how quickly concerns originating in global financial markets can affect Korean technology companies, even when demand for their products remains substantial.
The next test for AI investment
The divergence between TSMC's record earnings and the Korean market's sharp decline does not necessarily indicate a collapse in AI demand. Rather, it suggests that investors are applying greater scrutiny to the economics of the industry's expansion.
Future market assessments are likely to depend on several factors: whether major technology companies can sustain capital expenditure, whether AI services generate measurable returns, and whether semiconductor suppliers can maintain profitability as capacity expands.
For Korean semiconductor companies, strong demand for advanced memory and manufacturing technology remains an important advantage. Yet continued earnings growth alone may not be sufficient to protect valuations if investors become more concerned about financing costs and the profitability of their customers.
TSMC's results confirm that the AI semiconductor market continues to generate substantial revenue and profit. The Korean stock market's reaction points to a separate question: whether the broader AI investment ecosystem can convert unprecedented infrastructure spending into sustainable financial returns.

articles.summary: Global chipmaker sell-off deepens as enthusiasm for AI stocks wobbles  WPSD Local 6
articles.full_text:
(CNN) — Chipmaker stocks sold off sharply Thursday, sending investors in search of safety elsewhere, as a growing list of worries including rising borrowing costs and competition from China caused traders to sour on some AI investments.
A closely watched index of semiconductor chip stocks sank 2.5%, falling for the seventh day in a row. The drop in US chip stocks followed declines in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, which are global hubs for chipmakers.
Investors instead moved into other sectors of the market and snapped up government bonds in a flight to safety.
The Nasdaq Composite was down just 0.3%, paring earlier steeper declines. The index got a boost as investors bought the dip on some beleaguered names and software stocks rallied.
The tech-heavy index posted its worst decline since July on Wednesday, as shares of companies involved in the AI buildout, including chipmakers, tumbled.
“Worries about the AI buildout, bubbly valuations, lower-than-expected earnings growth at leading US frontier labs, Chinese competition, inflation and rates sent investors running for the covers,” Neil Wilson, a strategist at investment bank Saxo wrote in a note. He said that signs of slowing pace of revenue growth at Anthropic and OpenAI added to investor concerns.
Multiple news outlets reported that Anthropic, at an investor presentation ahead of its planned IPO expected in the near future, announced its sales grew 45% to $17 billion last quarter. Growth had more than doubled in the second quarter.
The Nasdaq and S&P 500 opened lower Thursday after fresh data showed wholesale inflation surged in September to its highest level in more than four years. The S&P then pared declines and was flat as investors rotated out of AI stocks and into other sectors.
Chip stocks rattle markets
Companies making semiconductor chips, which are critical for the AI boom, have experienced extraordinary growth this year from the data center buildout.
But after strong rallies earlier this year, and rising uncertainty about the data center buildout, stocks are taking a hit. The closely watched index of semiconductor stocks is down more than 20% since a peak in June.
Further hitting AI sentiment, C.C. Wei, the CEO of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest manufacturer of advanced chips, sounded a cautious note during an earnings call Thursday. He told analysts that rising component prices and macroeconomic uncertainty was challenging demand in some segments of the market.
The company’s shares finished 2% lower despite bumper earnings, contributing to a 3.5% decline in an index of Taiwan’s technology stocks.
South Korea’s Kospi led declines in Asia, finishing 7.6% lower on sharp drops in chipmakers SK Hynix (-11%) and Samsung Electronics (-9.5%). The scale of the decline triggered a circuit breaker, temporarily halting trading on the exchange — a frequent occurrence this year in a stock market dominated by just two stocks. Japan’s Nikkei finished 4.9% lower, with Hong Kong’s Hang Seng down 1%.
The Kospi, heavily weighted in chipmaker titans Samsung and SK Hynix, closed at a six-month low, erasing all of its gains since April. The Kospi in June was up as much as 116% on the year, but has since slumped more than a third, leaving year-to-date gains at 32%.
Adding to market jitters is growing competitive pressure from China, after Chinese semiconductor CXMT announced progress on advanced memory chips, raising doubts about the potential profitability of companies in the US and South Korea.
Rising rates and AI debt unsettle investors
The global retreat in technology stocks followed a sharp sell-off on Wall Street on Wednesday, after a strong US inflation report bolstered worries that rising interest rates will make it more expensive for companies to fund AI investments. Many AI companies are already heavily indebted.
CoreWeave, a data center and compute provider backed by Nvidia, is under scrutiny from analysts as rising interest rates complicate the outlook for the company, which has tens of billions of dollars of debt on its balance sheet.
CoreWeave shares dropped 15.5% on Wednesday. On Thursday, shares initially dropped before erasing losses after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told Bloomberg that he’s optimistic about the company.
Investor sentiment has soured over neoclouds like CoreWeave, or companies that provide specialized AI cloud infrastructure. Research firm Gartner published a report on Wednesday forecasting that over 80% of neocloud providers will cease operations by 2030, due to costs and lack of a unique business model.
Wall Street is also grappling with uncertainty over the political climate around data centers heading into the midterm elections. Investors are betting on an enormous buildout, and data center moratoriums or other slowdowns could hurt forecasts for returns on investments.
AI stock valuations have been volatile throughout the year. The biggest hyperscalers – Anthropic and OpenAI – remain privately traded, so investors look for clues about AI demand elsewhere. Any report that hints about slumping demand or higher-than-expected costs of building out AI infrastructure has frequently sent stocks on a rollercoaster ride.
“A slowdown in the AI infrastructure build out would imply a sharp slowdown in US growth expectations,” Mohit Kumar, chief European economist at Jefferies said in a note. The US is spending more on AI annually as a percentage of GDP than it did on building railways across the country in the 1800s, he noted.
But fears of a bubble suddenly popping have tended to be overblown.
“We expect the earnings season to justify that earnings and demand remain robust,” Kumar added. He cautioned, however, that Jefferies “would look to take some chips off the table” ahead of the midterms because a potential Democrat win in Congress “would be considered negative for the sector.”

The world’s memory chips are sold out. The companies that make them have just lost more than $1 trillion in market value.
Six of the largest memory and storage makers have shed about $1.09 trillion in combined value since the close on Friday, Oct. 2.
A Trillion Dollars Just Vanished From Memory Stocks
South Korea took the heaviest blow.
Seoul-listed shares of SK Hynix Inc. SKHY sank 11.1% on Thursday, its seventh straight loss, and have erased about 474.5 trillion won ($352.7 billion) since Oct. 2.
Shares now sit nearly 58% below their record. SK Hynix’s ADR was down 4.1% in New York trading on Thursday.
Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. SSNLF fell 9.5%, a loss of 462.6 trillion won ($343.8 billion) over the same period.
The Kospi index dropped 7.6% on the day.
In the U.S., Micron Technology Inc. MU fell 4.4% to $874.14 at the open, heading for a sixth straight decline.
It has lost $227.1 billion in value since Oct. 2. Sandisk Corp. SNDK dropped 6.6% to $1,311.42, bringing its loss to $59.1 billion over the period.
| Company | Change since Oct. 2 | Value lost | From record high | 
|---|---|---|---|
| SK Hynix Inc. | -31.5% | $352.7 billion | -57.8% | 
| Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. ( | -23.9% | $343.8 billion | -43.9% | 
| Micron Technology Inc. MU | -18.7% | $227.1 billion | -30.3% |

| Sandisk Corp. SNDK | -23.8% | $59.1 billion | -44.3% | 
| Western Digital Corp. WDC | -17.5% | $27.2 billion | -57.2% | 
Three Fears at Once
The first is AI spending.
Anthropic’s annualized revenue reached $67.2 billion in the third quarter, Bloomberg reported. That is only modestly above the $65 billion pace it had hit at the end of July.
It was the second warning sign in as many weeks. Chip stocks had already slid last week amid confusion over how fast OpenAI’s annualized revenue is really growing.
The second is China.
Earlier this week, Counterpoint Research reported that China’s Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., known as YMTC, has become the world’s third-largest maker of NAND flash, the memory used to store data in phones, laptops and data centers.
"China will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028," Elon Musk wrote on X on Thursday.
He was replying to a summary of a Maeil Business Newspaper column.
The column warned that South Korea’s memory boom could face oversupply from 2029 as new capacity comes online. That leaves the country two to three years to build new growth industries.
The stakes are national. South Korea’s semiconductor exports jumped 263% to $60.3 billion in September, according to government data.
That is nearly half of the country’s record $120.9 billion in total exports.
D.A. Davidson’s Gil Luria sees the same split. "If there’s an impact, there’s some impact on SK Hynix and Samsung. It’s not on Micron," he told CNBC.
The third is rates. Two hotter-than-expected inflation reports in two days revived fears of a Federal Reserve rate hike in October, and that weighed on tech stocks more broadly.
On Wednesday, consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier in September, above the 3.6% economists expected. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose to 2.6%, against 2.5% expected.
On Thursday, producer prices, which track what businesses charge each other, jumped 1.3% in September. That is more than double the 0.5% forecast. Core producer prices rose 0.7%, against 0.3% expected.
Higher rates make it more expensive to borrow for the data centers that buy these chips.
Read Also: SK Hynix’s Worst 7-Day Loss Since 2008: AI Bubble Bursting Or Historical Opportunity?
TSMC Says Demand Is Still Running Ahead
The world’s largest contract chipmaker points the other way.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. TSM reported third-quarter revenue of $46.72 billion on Thursday, above its own guidance. It raised its 2026 growth outlook for the third time this year, to about 44%.
Cantor Fitzgerald analyst C.J. Muse called it "yet another very bullish report." He said TSMC is seeing AI demand that "continues to run well ahead of supply."
The stock fell anyway. TSMC’s U.S.-listed shares dropped 4.3% to $411.71 at the open.
SOXX on Track for an 8-Day Losing Streak
The memory selloff pushed the iShares Semiconductor ETF SOXX down 3.3% to $502.20 shortly after Thursday’s open.
The fund is on track for its eighth straight loss, down 14.8% over that stretch.
An eight-session losing streak has happened only seven times since 2001. The last time was September 2015.
History offers some comfort.
In six of the seven past eight-day losing streaks, SOXX was higher a year later, with an average gain of 21.1%.
The exception was January 2008, when the fund fell another 42.5% over the following year.

The benchmark KOSPI tumbled 7.57 percent to close at 5,554.22, marking its steepest decline since July 28. The index extended its losing streak to seven consecutive sessions, shedding 21 percent over the period.
The selloff came as U.S. inflation concerns and renewed doubts about the profitability of artificial intelligence (AI)-led investment battered semiconductor shares, particularly Samsung Electronics and SK hynix.
The KOSPI opened 5.59 percent lower at 5,673.01 and plunged as much as 9.29 percent to an intraday low of 5,450.81 before recovering some losses late in the session. It finished at its lowest closing level since April 7.
Foreign investors sold 3.63 trillion won (US$2.7 billion) worth of KOSPI shares, extending their selling streak to eight consecutive sessions. Retail investors bought 1.29 trillion won, while institutions purchased 1.69 trillion won throughout Thursday's session.
The losses were concentrated in the country's two largest chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK hynix as investors reassessed the profitability of massive AI infrastructure investment amid rising borrowing costs.
The selloff followed the release of U.S. consumer price data overnight showing that inflation rose faster than expected in September. Consumer prices increased 3.7 percent from a year earlier, exceeding the market forecast of 3.6 percent. Core inflation also came in above expectations at 2.6 percent.
The figures revived concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again, potentially increasing financing costs for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure.
Questions over the sustainability of AI spending also intensified after research firm Gartner warned of a widening gap between projected infrastructure investment and the revenue needed to justify it.
The concerns weighed on U.S. technology stocks overnight. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.88 percent, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped 4.30 percent, extending its losing streak to six sessions.
Samsung Electronics closed 9.48 percent lower at 210,000 won after briefly falling to 204,500 won. SK hynix plunged 11.06 percent to 1,262,000 won, having touched an intraday low of 1,238,000 won.
The two companies, whose combined market capitalization accounts for nearly half of the KOSPI, amplified the index's decline as investors retreated from memory chipmakers that had benefited from the AI boom.
Other technology stocks also suffered heavy losses. Samsung Electro-Mechanics, a major electronic components supplier, plunged 15.36 percent, while SK Square, the largest shareholder of SK hynix, dropped 10.21 percent.
The weakness extended to automakers, battery manufacturers and industrial companies. Hyundai Motor fell alongside Samsung SDI and Doosan Enerbility as selling pressure spread beyond the semiconductor sector.
Some defensive stocks bucked the downturn. Samsung Biologics gained 5.50 percent, while Celltrion advanced 1.28 percent and Hana Financial Group rose 0.66 percent.
By sector, electrical and electronics shares dropped 10.13 percent, while medical and precision equipment stocks fell 8.87 percent. Pharmaceutical shares rose 2.65 percent and food and beverage stocks gained 2.05 percent.
The severe decline triggered a sell-side trading curb shortly after the opening bell, temporarily suspending program sell orders. As the index's losses exceeded 8 percent in afternoon trading, a circuit breaker was activated at around 12:30 p.m., halting all KOSPI trading for 20 minutes.
The market turmoil prompted the Financial Services Commission to hold an emergency meeting Thursday afternoon. Financial authorities urged caution over excessive borrowing and leveraged investment amid heightened volatility.
The junior KOSDAQ also suffered a sharp decline, falling 7.65 percent or 63.06 points to close at 760.82. It dropped below the 800 mark at the opening and extended its losing streak to six sessions.
The KOSDAQ opened at 784.45 and fell as low as 745.43, a decline of 9.52 percent before paring some losses toward the close.
A sell-side trading curb was activated shortly after the market opened, followed by a circuit breaker at around 12:20 p.m. as losses exceeded 8 percent. Trading was suspended for 20 minutes, marking the first such halt since July 29.
Unlike the KOSPI, where foreign selling dominated, overseas investors bought 217.7 billion won worth of KOSDAQ shares. Retail investors sold 66.7 billion won, while institutions unloaded 163.2 billion won.
Semiconductor equipment and battery-related companies were among the hardest hit.
Jusung Engineering, a semiconductor equipment manufacturer, plunged 14.97 percent, while EcoPro BM, a producer of cathode materials for rechargeable batteries, lost 9.10 percent. Its parent company EcoPro also declined sharply.
Biotechnology and robotics stocks remained under pressure. Alteogen, a developer of drug-delivery technologies, fell 4.90 percent, while Rainbow Robotics, a manufacturer of industrial and collaborative robots, dropped 9.44 percent.
The South Korean won weakened against the dollar, with the exchange rate reaching 1,344.6 won per dollar at around 3:30 p.m.
Asian markets also retreated, despite their losses were smaller than South Korea. Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 4.90 percent to 64,425.95, while China's Shanghai Composite declined about 1.6 percent to 3,707.48. Taiwan's benchmark index dropped 3.41 percent.
Investors are closely watching upcoming U.S. economic data, the Federal Reserve's policy meeting later this month and quarterly earnings from major technology companies for clues to whether the selloff will deepen.
