articles.title: MUFG wades back into Japanese bonds with eye on policy risks - The Business Times
articles.summary: MUFG wades back into Japanese bonds with eye on policy risks  The Business Times
articles.full_text:
The chief executive of the bank’s global markets business says it has started ‘exploratory purchases’ of 10-year JGBs at around 3.1%
[TOKYO] Japan’s biggest bank is tentatively getting back into the country’s benchmark government bonds, even as it remains concerned that yields could further spike due to fiscal and monetary policies in the nation.
“We plan to rebuild our position gradually going forward while carefully assessing interest-rate levels,” said Atsushi Yamashita, chief executive of MUFG Bank’s global markets business.
Yamashita expects Japan’s 10-year government bond yields to peak at about 3.2 per cent, just above the three-decade high of 3.115 per cent reached earlier this month.
But Yamashita remains wary that yields could climb higher if the Bank of Japan (BOJ) struggles to contain inflation or Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi fails to convince investors that she can maintain a grip on government finances.
“We don’t yet think risks of a further yield rise have been completely eliminated,” he said in his first interview since taking the role at the core unit of Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group.
Global investors are grappling with a surge in yields in major economies, where questions over fiscal sustainability are gaining more urgency along with rising prices fueled by the prolonged Middle East conflict.
MUFG and rival Japanese banks are being watched closely for signs of a shift in their cautious stance toward the nation’s bonds, whose value has been falling steadily as interest rates rise.
Yamashita, who took the position in April, is responsible for managing the lender’s securities investments. MUFG’s banking and trust bank units had a combined portfolio of more than 85 trillion yen (US$537 billion) as of June.
MUFG has been trimming its holdings of longer-term Japanese government bonds (JGBs) in recent years, reducing its exposure to rising interest rates. The average duration of its JGB holdings fell to 1.2 years as of June, from 3.1 as of September last year.
Yamashita said that the bank started “exploratory purchases” of 10-year JGBs at around 3.1 per cent.
While his base case is for yields to peak at 3.2 per cent, he noted that there’s a risk that they climb to the mid-to-high 3 per cent range, potentially driven by the policy paths of the central bank and the government.
Ten-year JGB yields fell 5 basis points to 2.945 per cent on Thursday (Oct 15) morning in Tokyo, dropping more than other tenors.
Markets are watching whether Takaichi maintains fiscal discipline as she carries out her ambitious economic growth agenda.
In a country with the highest ratio of debt to gross domestic product in the developed world, questions remain over how the government will finance outlays and a temporary tax cut on food items in Budget proposals to be unveiled toward the end of the year.
“It is important from the standpoint of maintaining market confidence to conduct fiscal policy without relying too heavily on optimistic growth scenarios,” Yamashita said.
While acknowledging that the country’s finances are improving thanks to an inflation-driven increase in tax revenue, he added: “Markets are looking not only at the current situation, but also at what lies ahead.”
The Bank of Japan’s policy outlook also carries risks, as soaring energy costs and a weak yen spur inflation.
“The market is most concerned about a scenario in which the pace of rate hikes fails to keep up with inflationary pressures, leaving the Bank of Japan behind the curve,” said Yamashita.
He said that the BOJ’s next rate hike is likely to come in December, followed by more in roughly three-month intervals. While he expects the terminal rate to reach around 2 per cent from 1.25 per cent now, it may go higher depending on inflation prospects.
Even as MUFG gradually builds up its yen bond holdings, Yamashita ruled out repatriation, which involves selling assets overseas to invest more at home. “If yields become sufficiently attractive in light of factors such as where the rate-hiking cycle ultimately peaks, there would be scope to increase our foreign-bond investments as well.”
MUFG has little exposure to European sovereign bonds, including French debt, Yamashita pointed out.
Volatility in European bond markets is likely to remain elevated for now, but the bloc is unlikely to spiral toward a situation similar to the debt crisis that engulfed it around 15 years ago, he said. “The current concerns are centred on the fiscal and political situations of specific countries and haven’t spread into broader concerns about the stability of the region’s financial system.”
Still, Yamashita added that France’s fiscal and political challenges that have fuelled a bond market rout offer a lesson for Japan. He pointed out: “How to contain the fiscal deficit while debt-servicing costs are being pushed up by rising rates should serve as cautionary example for Japan. It’s likely to face the same problem in the future.” BLOOMBERG

Qualcomm (QCOM) and Broadcom (AVGO) shares are in focus after a Bloomberg report said ByteDance is close to a deal to buy custom AI chips from Taiwan’s MediaTek for its data centers.
MediaTek would supply ByteDance with application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), which are designed for particular computing tasks. MediaTek is a major vendor for Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs).
The deal is a competitive signal for Qualcomm and Broadcom. ByteDance agreed earlier this year to buy millions of AI chips from Qualcomm, while it would give MediaTek a stronger foothold in a market where Broadcom is already well established.
Nvidia (NVDA) could also face pressure if ByteDance shifts more AI workloads to custom ASICs, reducing its reliance on GPUs, although U.S. export restrictions on advanced chips are already forcing Chinese companies to look for alternatives.
ASIC Chips Market
Demand for ASICs has grown as AI companies seek alternatives to general-purpose GPUs, with major cloud providers such as Amazon and Google and AI developers increasingly investing in their own chips to cut costs.
Bloomberg reported that ByteDance is considering capital expenditure of up to $70 billion this year, more than double last year’s total, as it builds out its AI infrastructure.
MediaTek expects AI-chip sales to reach about $2 billion this year and is targeting 15% of an $80 billion market next year, according to Bloomberg.
Global Chip Rout
Global semiconductor stocks extended their selloff on Thursday as hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data heightened interest-rate concerns, compounding worries about AI spending and intensifying Chinese competition.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell for a seventh consecutive session on Wednesday and dropped 1.7% overnight, while South Korea’s Kospi tumbled more than 7% on Thursday, with Samsung and SK Hynix among the biggest decliners.

On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘bearish’ for QCOM, and ‘extremely bearish’ for AVGO and NVDA.
“NVDA all I can say is the stock market is bipolar. One day Nvidia is changing planet earth and next world is going bankrupt. The amount of manipulation is unreal. It’s not even weeks but days that story lines change,” a trader wrote.

- SK Hynix shares have fallen 20% this month.
- The company’s U.S. unit is tying plans for a new NAND factory to U.S. approval for additional chipmaking equipment shipments to China.
- Rising U.S. inflation, concerns over AI spending and growing competition from Chinese chipmakers have added to pressure on semiconductor stocks.
South Korea's SK Hynix is seeking U.S. approval to export chipmaking equipment to China to increase production there as a condition of building a factory in America, Reuters reported late Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
SKHY stock fell 6.5% in overnight trading late Wednesday, after a similar drop in the regular session, amid a global selloff in chip stocks over fresh concerns about the durability of AI spending and the high valuations of AI-linked companies.
SKHY stock has dropped 20% so far this month, heading for its worst monthly move since its Nasdaq listing in July. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for the stock remained ‘bullish,’ unchanged over the past seven days.
Solidigm, SK Hynix’s U.S. unit, wants to install equipment to manufacture NAND flash memory chips in unused space at SK Hynix’s facility in Dalian, China, and is seeking a U.S. export license for additional equipment from Lam Research, Applied Materials and KLA Corp.
Solidigm is now making its plan to build a new U.S. NAND factory contingent on the license, Reuters reported. Expanded production from China, through the Dalian factory, would help Solidigm fund the U.S. facility, the report added.
The move comes as the Donald Trump administration pushes foreign semiconductor manufacturers, including SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, to expand manufacturing in the U.S.
US Export Restrictions Complicate Plans
Last year, the Commerce Department revoked exemptions that let SK Hynix and Samsung ship U.S. equipment to their Chinese factories without individual licenses. The department later allowed equipment shipments to keep existing operations running but said it did not expect to approve licenses for capacity expansions or technology upgrades, Reuters reported.
SK Hynix received a license covering its Dalian facility for 2026, but the authorization limits equipment quantities. Reuters reported that approval for additional equipment in 2027 remains pending.
Global Chip Rout
Global semiconductor stocks extended their selloff on Thursday as hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data heightened interest-rate concerns, compounding worries about AI spending and intensifying Chinese competition.
U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% year-over-year in September, up from 3.4% in August. articles.title: Japan needs higher interest rates - Interest.co.nz
articles.summary: Japan needs higher interest rates  Interest.co.nz
articles.full_text:
On a recent visit to Sapporo, the city on Japan’s northern island where my parents came from, my wife and I found gentle people, mild autumn days, and excellent food. As tourists who live and work in the United States, we also enjoyed very low prices: lunch at a high-quality restaurant cost only about $20 per person. While that was convenient for us, like so many other tourists who have headed to Japan to take advantage of favorable exchange rates, the cheap yen (yen yasu) has been hard on Japan’s economy.
To understand the pressure Japan is under, it is worth looking at the purchasing-power-parity equilibrium exchange rate—the rate at which a representative basket of goods and services would cost the same across two countries. This month, the OECD reports a PPP equilibrium exchange rate between Japan and the United States of around 93 yen per dollar. That is a far cry from the actual yen-dollar exchange rate, which has been hovering in the 150–160 range.
This means that goods produced in Japan cost much less than goods produced in the US. As a result, Japanese exporters enjoy high demand and strong profit margins, but importers are under severe pressure. The weak yen also hurts Japanese consumers, as it creates strong incentives to raise prices: With imported goods more expensive, domestic producers know that their output will find buyers, and importers might pass their mounting costs on to buyers.
Japan used to have the opposite problem. In the early 1980s, it was a dominant economy experiencing strong growth. But the 1985 Plaza Accord, under which major economies agreed to take coordinated action to strengthen their currencies vis-à-vis the US dollar, changed everything. After the accord was implemented, the PPP exchange rate was higher than the actual exchange rate, reaching almost double in 1995.
The strong yen (yen daka) persisted for decades, contributing to chronic deflation and stagnant growth. During this period, a visit to Tokyo strained tourists’ pocketbooks, Japanese goods found few customers abroad, and Japan’s once-formidable industries struggled. The situation deteriorated further around the 2008 global economic crisis, when the US embraced monetary easing.
In the decades after the Plaza Accord, Bank of Japan (BOJ) governors (with the possible exception of Toshihiko Fukui) consistently failed to loosen monetary policy in line with changing economic conditions. Deflationary pressures intensified.
After returning to power in 2012, Prime Minister Abe Shinzō sought to turn things around with an economic-reform package (I served as an adviser), which came to be known as Abenomics. This package included a recommendation for monetary expansion, which then-BOJ Governor Haruhiko Kuroda embraced.
Now, conditions have changed. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the US experienced a surge in inflation, which forced the US Federal Reserve to abandon monetary expansion and raise interest rates. As the dollar strengthened, and the US-Japan interest-rate differential widened, the yen depreciated in value, and deflationary forces gave way to inflationary pressures.
When circumstances change, so, too, must policy. For the BOJ today, this means pursuing monetary tightening in order to reduce the domestic money supply, and raising the interest rate.
To some extent, Japanese policymakers seem to recognize this. After keeping the short-term interest rate around 1% for some time, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25% last month. This is high for Japan (the highest in 31 years, to be precise). But with the US short-term money market pushing the interest rate close to 4%, and more US rate hikes likely, it is not nearly enough. Speculators continue to exploit the interest-rate differential via the so-called carry trade (borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad).
Under the gold standard or a fixed exchange rate, if a major country pursued monetary expansion, another, weaker country might need to reduce its money supply and raise its interest rate. Under a flexible exchange-rate regime, however, an expansion in one country should be met with a (moderate) expansion in another, just as tightening should be met with tightening.
We know that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Japanese Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki are communicating about fiscal and monetary matters. Ultimately, however, monetary policy must be pursued autonomously, with BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda doing what is best for Japan’s economy. Under the current circumstances, that means reducing the money supply and raising interest rates more aggressively.

articles.title: Taiwan to Join US China Chip Curbs, Seek Criminal Penalties for AI Chip Smuggling - bloomingbit
articles.summary: Taiwan to Join US China Chip Curbs, Seek Criminal Penalties for AI Chip Smuggling  bloomingbit
articles.full_text:
Summary
- Taiwan said it will tighten export controls in line with US restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors, AI chips, and AI servers to China, while pursuing criminal penalties for illegal shipments to the mainland.
- If the new rules are introduced, Taiwan would secure a legal basis to directly impose criminal penalties on the smuggling of AI chips to China, making the measure a key export-control step aimed at preventing technology leaks and strengthening national security.
- Taiwan said it is also pursuing investment to build an AI semiconductor supply chain in the US, with plans to raise billions of dollars to create a local supply chain that AI hardware companies including Nvidia can use.
Forecast Trend Report by Period
Taiwan is moving to tighten export controls on artificial intelligence chips and servers in line with US restrictions on advanced semiconductor sales to China, and is seeking to criminalize illegal shipments to the mainland.
Bloomberg reported on October 16 that Taiwan Economy Minister Kuo Jyh-huei said in an interview that the government plans to add AI servers and advanced semiconductors to its export control list. Once the measures take effect, exporting restricted AI chip equipment to China without a license would be subject to criminal penalties under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
In the interview, conducted on October 12, Kuo said some future export control measures would be aligned with US rules because Taiwan had made substantial commitments in a mutual trade agreement signed with the US this year. He did not provide a timeline for implementation.
The move comes as Washington tightens export restrictions aimed at blocking advanced AI semiconductors from reaching China. The US has restricted exports of high-performance AI chips made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. to China, but Chinese companies are known to have obtained such products through third countries and other channels. US authorities believe Nvidia chips worth billions of dollars have entered China illegally in recent years.
Taiwan currently lacks a provision allowing authorities to treat the unauthorized export of AI chips to China as a criminal offense in itself. While officials have warned about potential violations of US export controls, prosecutors have had to rely on other domestic laws when pursuing smuggling cases.
If the new rules are adopted, Taiwan would gain a direct legal basis to criminally punish the smuggling of advanced AI chips into China. That would make the measure one of the key export-control steps under President Lai Ching-te's government to prevent technology leaks and strengthen national security.
Taiwan has previously said it would respond to US concerns over export controls. The tighter rules also reflect a broader push to deepen economic and security cooperation with Washington while limiting the outflow of advanced technology to China.
Separately, Taiwan is also pursuing investment to build an AI semiconductor supply chain in the US. Kuo told Bloomberg this week that the government plans to raise billions of dollars to develop industrial parks in the US. The goal is to establish a local supply chain that AI hardware companies, including Nvidia, can use.
